chunks: LiPo storage charge. The question: What is storage charging?
Storage charge is how full you should leave a lithium battery when you will not use it for a while. The answer is about 3. 8 volts per cell, roughly half full.
Storing it full wears the cell out faster. Storing it empty is risky, because the battery slowly loses charge by itself and may end up too low to recover.
Think of a spring. Held fully compressed for months, a spring gets tired and loses its bounce. Left fully loose, it is fine.
A battery differs here, because it slowly leaks charge on its own, and an empty one can leak past its safe limit. The best place to rest it is partway, with margin on both sides.
The storage band sits mid-curve, about 3. 77 to 3. 84 volts. Above it the cell is increasingly reactive; below it the margin to the damaging region shrinks.
The curve's steep foot below 10 % is where drift hurts most.
State of charge (SoC): how full the battery is, as a percentage ("Determining state of charge and why it's hard"). Storage voltage: about 3. 8 to 3.
85 volts per cell, which is roughly 50 to 60% SoC ("LiPo cell voltage range and why"). Self-discharge: charge a cell loses just sitting, a few percent a month.
Parasitic drain: tiny currents drawn by attached electronics even when the device is off.
Calendar aging: wear that happens with time, faster when the cell is full and warm ("LiPo aging and end of life").
A 2 Ah cell stored at 3. 8 volts (about 54%) holds about 0. 54 times 2000 equals 1080 milliamp hours above empty.
Self-discharge of 3% a month, about 60 milliamp hours, would take roughly 18 months to drain it.
A parasitic drain of 1 milliamps is much worse: 1080 over 1 equals 1080 hours, or about 45 days.
A full cell has more charge to lose before it runs flat, but it ages faster, especially in the heat. That is the whole idea.
"Storage charge is the level you leave a LiPo at when it's not in use, about 3. 8 volts per cell, roughly 50 percent.
Full charge accelerates calendar aging and gas, especially when warm, and leaves more stored energy if something fails.
Empty is worse in a different way: self-discharge and parasitic drain can pull the cell below about 2.
5 to 3 volts into over-discharge, which damages the anode and, deep enough, dissolves the copper collector. So store around 3.
8 volts, cool and dry, away from flammable things, and check it every few months."
